blocks.x: Okay. Today is January 17th. We are at 1433 Dolphin, the home of Mona McMurray. We have Sing Miller and Kid Sheik here. We've just been making some tapes of some of Sing's records. And now we'd like to talk a little bit about Sing's life history. When were you

born Sing? 1913, June the 17th. And where? 546 Lines Street. The house I was born is still there, painted green, in the middle of the block. You still see it? See, there was another week. Where did you go to school first? I was Lutheran School.
Where was that? Washington in the Drys. Was that when you started the first grade there? I started first grade

at Miss Mary Steele. My school teacher still lives. Who was that? Mary Steele. Was that a special school or one? A special school. A house school. It wasn't a regular building. It was a house school. And how long did you go to school? To what grade? I went as far as 10th grade. In the 10th grade. And then what did you do? When I started playing music, I took lessons from Professor Victor. My mother used to give me 15 cents. I'd buy an apple on a stick, give him a dime.
How old were you when you first started playing the piano?
You were about 14 then, huh? Something like that. Where did you get your first piano? Mother bought a piano for $10. Yeah? Where did you get a piano for $10?
Well, during them times, people were throwing pianos away. Oh, they were? I used to be a two-figure piano player. You just started banging? Yeah, banging by myself. Always could play the blues.
You just started picking it up by yourself? Yeah, picking it by myself. Then how did you meet this Victor where you started taking lessons?
When I went to LaFontaine School. You met him? Yeah. He was a school teacher. He played everything.
Wait, he taught piano or he just played? Yeah, he taught piano, cyzbole, and trumpet. Well, how did you come to decide you were going to take lessons from him?
Well, everybody else was doing something, so I wanted to do something too.
And where were you working when you started to work? What was your first job?
My first job was a dishwasher, washing dishes. Where was that? Down in half a week. Wow. At Manali's Restaurant.
Oh, Manali's? Manali's, yeah. Manali's is still operating, huh?
Yeah, Manali's still there. All the Manali's days were about, with Pascal.
And when was that? Do you remember? Do you remember?
About 19... About 1932, stuff like that.
Right. And how long did you work there?
I worked there until probation was over. When the probation authority I delivered the first bottle of beer.
You did?
Nixon beer.
The first bottle of beer? Nixon.
I delivered the first bottle of beer in the city.
How did that come about? What were you doing?
That's the first place to deliver.
You mean you got a job driving a delivery?
Riding a bicycle.
Oh, you rode a bicycle?
Couldn't get on a bicycle. Had to get on the curb to get on a bicycle. Legs too short.
Oh. But you managed to ride. What, you delivered beer? Just beer or anything?
Beer and oysters. Oysters on the tray.
Oh. Well, what company were you working for then?
That was a restaurant.
Nestill and see? Manali's too? Yeah. Oh, you were promoted from dishwasher to delivery boy? Yeah. And then you delivered beer?
A dollar and a half, three meals a day.
A dollar and a half?
All I could eat, all I could steal.
Oh, and how long altogether did you work for Manali? About four years. And then where did you work?
I worked at a Meister's truck store. What did you do there?
Delivery boy. Delivery boy? How long did you work there?
I worked for him twelve years. Twelve years? Wow. Twelve years. I've seen all his churn raised up. Uh-huh.
How much a week did he get?
Four hours a week.
Dude, that was a big high pay, huh?
Four hours. Then he could live high.
Four hours. And he'd get the ice cream freezer. Every day.
Every day, you get all the ice cream you wanted? All I could eat. When did you get married, see?
I got married in 34.
And what were you working at for a living when you got married? At the drugstore. You still working at the drugstore? You got married on the four dollars a week?
On that four dollars a week. I was paying 60 cents a week and couldn't pay that.
60 cents a week?
The landlord come on Saturday for a rent, I'd give him 50 cents. I'd say, I owe you a dime. 50 cents a week?
Where were you living then?
I lived on Water Street.
And the rent was 60 cents a week? Cost of Oakland and Water, yeah.
4033 Water Street. And what kind of a place did you have?
I had one room.

Cooked, eaten, everything else. That one room. Had my clothes in the egg box. Cooked on a grate. Cooked with tar blocks. Train passed by with chocolate with storm cool on. I unloaded in my yard. That's how I kept my family warm.
Oh, you mean they just dropped coal in the yard?
No, the coal. Coal box passed by. I'd get up on that toilet cool over in my yard.
Oh. And then, and how long did you live there at that 60 cents? You paid 50 cents for him?
I stayed there until my first child was born.
And when was that?
Well, he was born, he was born in the last part of March 8, 35, 34.
And then where did you move to?
Moved another hour, two hours a week. Two hours a week?
Oh, that was high rent.
That was room in the kitchen, two hours a week. Wow. Landon put my mind, I made too much noise. What, playing the piano?
Yeah. He didn't like to hear you practice? No.
Me, I'm playing the ball.
But what, for practicing or just playing? Practice. Well, in the meantime, while all this was going on, you were just playing music on the side? Yeah. And where did you play? Where was your practice?
My first job was at the UK Ball on the 7th. Made 60 cents.
60 cents, yeah. 60 cents. Who did you play with?
I played with the Hickman Brothers.
All right, and who else played?
John Bruce, Julius Simpson, Buddy Charles. And way around 1940 when I met Cheek at the Cotton Club.
Mm-hmm. And this first job, was it a dance or?
No, just a peakeasy.
Oh, I see. And you just sat there and played? I sat there and played. Uh-huh. What did you make there? Just tips or did you get paid?
No tips, no, no tips. 60 cents what you made. Oh, for the long? Hot dog man was on the outside waiting for you to buy hot dogs. Out there. Out there.
How much should he charge you for the hot dog? 15 cents for hot dogs. Wow, it took a whole quarter of your night's pay.

And you needed two hot dogs to get full, so I got them with 30 cents. Oh, and then where did you play after that? Well, after that, I went out there by Mama Lou with Clayton. Oh. Out on Lakefront, Kit Clayton. And what year was that?
Do you remember?
I was doing a, I was doing a, I was in Millen Boy, you know, around 37, 30. Late 30. Yeah, late 30. Yeah.
And when did you meet Sheik? In 41.
In 41?
What, just, you met him on a job or?
No, I played with Sheik in 41. Uh-huh. Cotton Club. What did you play there? Yeah, she had Albert DeLone and his brother playing Saints Ball with him there.
And who else was playing? I don't remember. Different fellas and Schmell.
You had so many different, and how much did you get paid there?
I forgot.
Sometime we didn't get nothing.
Sometime we didn't get nothing. You see for yourself. You see for yourself.
Oh, in other words, you were supposed to try to get what tips you could get, huh? No, if he ain't made nothing.
If he ain't made nothing, you couldn't get nothing. Oh, it depends on what he made.
At night. Oh, he meant, you see for yourself there was nobody here.
Yeah.
Oh, I see. Well, how long did you all play together at the Cotton Club?
I played a good ball. You know, so everything. Got a lot of getting this scattered around, you know. And then?
After I left Sheik, I went down there by the next corner, by the Big Apple, started playing with George Gato.
And how long did you play there?
I played down there about two, three months. That was a wine jack there.
And who else played in that band?
Oh, I'm glad.
You don't remember?
I know Julius Simpson played drum, I know. Tony played trumpet. Tony, right? Tony.
Oh, Tony Fulcic.
Tony, yeah. And what was it? Then I went with Earl Fawcett.
And when was that?

I started with him at the Carmel Club on Blyer Street. His wife used to come in and bring red beans and rice at night. Feed the band? And she played a drum while you eat. Oh, really? Oh, she'd bring his dinner?
Yeah, you had to bring your dinner on them jobs.
You had to bring two shirts.
Bring two shirts? You sweat, yeah.
Oh.
And then she, was she a good drummer? Yeah, she played nice drums.

She played really nice drums. Yeah. She played time. Well, during that time Joe Betty was playing trumpet then. Nice trumpet player. But Joe Betty was using dope and every time he'd go on a job he'd pull his arm for that dope. That's for running him crazy. I've never seen Joe with a woman in my life. Never. And Joe was a good leader.
Yeah. And when did he die?
He's eleven.
He's still in it? He's still in it. What's he doing?
He's selling that wheat.
Oh, he's, he come out for the preservation hall sometimes.
Yeah, well he's selling wheat but I got a wheat from him this week. He was passing the handbook.
He was working at first.
Oh, yeah, sure. He was working at first in Daniel for drinks. Well, he doesn't play music anymore, though. No, no, no.
I'm not sure I said there was a good choice.

Yeah, that's right. I remember we were, yeah, no, we were just walking to the bar. We were just walking to the hall and you walked by and handed you the paper. Well then, uh, seeing, what are you doing now for a living? I mean... Me? Yeah, I mean, you do, you do a lot of carpentry and...
I was human finishing.
That's what your profession is. That's my profession.
That's my profession.
When did you learn that?
I learned that from working with Bo Brothers.
Oh, when did you go to work for Bo Brothers? After I came on the service.
I know. Forty-five.
Oh, no. I know. I used to take pictures of all that stuff they were doing when they were making those overpasses and underpasses. Yeah. And you learned that on the job, like on the job training?
I learned that on the job. And then I did all that job then I worked for myself.
And you still have your own business?
My own business. I worked for me.
Well, you do other things too, don't you? You do carpentry.
I don't do no painting. I do carpentry work.
You do carpentry work? What else?
Mechanic work.
I let the mother go out.
Most of your mechanic work is done on your truck, fixing it, huh?
T-79. Don't leave me, my lady.
Don't leave me.

Yeah, but that's one thing I'm about to say. When he's drinking, he doesn't drive that truck. He leaves it right there. Remember the night you were too high and you did take the truck and you ran in the back of a taxi?
That's right. He didn't have to work.
How long have you been playing at Preservation Hall?
Six years.
Well, who did you play with first then?
I started there with you.
Oh, when Sheik first started?

I started there with Sheik. Yeah. And then you started... Sheik I went to work with Kit Thomas, from Kit Thomas to Percy. From, now I was in Prince Band before I went with him, Percy Band. I started with Percy.
Now you're playing with Thomas and who else?
I play with Billy and Dee Dee when he was sick.
Yeah, you're playing Billy's playing. Yeah. And who else you play with?
With Percy.
Just with Percy, that's all.
Sheik plays.
Yeah, on one Sheik plays. On the rare occasions that Sheik plays there, yeah. And that's about all you do now. That's all. Do you work steady every day? I mean, aw.
No, no. Nobody hires you at this age steady.
But I mean, do you get a fair amount of work, enough to live on? Enough to live on, yeah. Keep you in beer and stuff. Yeah. Where are you living now, Singh?
22-02, that was sheik. Mm-hmm.
What kind of plans you got for the future, if any?
You're going to buy me a house and sit down.
You're going to buy me a house and sit down and collect your Social Security, huh? That's right. You got a little way to go yet, though, huh? No, I don't have that many years to go.
What, let's see, 13? How old are you now?
I'm 58. 58. Well, you got four more years. I'll be naked.
Yeah.
Remember what we were talking about earlier, but— I'll be back. I'll be back.
You'll be back.
Yeah, you'll be back. Yeah, you'll be back.
Yeah, you'll be back. Yeah, you'll be back.

Yeah, we were talking about Dave Oxley when he carried him off in the ambulance. I'll be back, I'll be back. Well, remember we were talking a little while ago about mentioning about Cap, and talking about all the different people, all the musicians who have died, and they've all been playing at Preservation Hall at one time or another. And—
One time somebody dies, somebody said they need a piano player up there. I said, you got two or three of them up there already, don't need me.
Yeah, what other piano players who played at Preservation Hall at the time?
Well, I played back, he played there. I played there.
Sunday. Sunday, you go play there.
Well, Sunday I played more at Dixieland though, didn't I?
Yeah, but he played there. Yeah. I couldn't have that much, but he played there.
But you know, that is kind of strange, aren't you? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
many piano players.
Most of them are all the musicians. Well you see, what happened most to all the four musicians is the one that played at the reservation.

That has a lot to do with it because so many of the musicians who just weren't doing anything and then started playing at the hall, and most of them are up in age, and some of them were sick like Joe Watkins, he had that stroke, and then there isn't much anymore to do. If you can't walk in a parade you just don't play, and there aren't that many gigs around anymore.
Preservation of Holland and Dixonite.
Preservation of Holland and Dixonite, and that's it. Only two. That's all that's left, unless you get a tour. Not too many of those.
I've been fortunate most every year.
You've been lucky about that. That brought you through to your Social Security. Now you get your what, $68?
$68 a month. Fingin' on a raise. You're gonna need it. Well it's a fool to put that up there at one double O. Yeah.
Well that will leave Sheik some money over. He has to take a cab home every night when he stays out like things are so bad and where he lives.
I'm $62 a month. Just on cab? Just cab. Now I come on the bus, I catch the bus in the evening coming.
Well that takes care of the other age for you. Yeah. They keep raising the bus fare, it'll be cheaper to take a cab both ways.
Yeah, bus fare and cab fare, that eats up my pension.

Well my rent, eat me up, $61 every month. I'm looking for the go in there one night, the roof be done fell in on me and I'm a shoe out of there, I own a house. You, you, you don't fix nothing. How many rooms you got there?
Two rooms in the kitchen. Two rooms in the kitchen?
Sixty?
Yeah, sixty-one rooms. I got five rooms here for seventy-five.
But I'm working. If I had five rooms in my house I'd have me a den, a bowl and everything else in there. Yeah, because you could build anything.
Yeah. Why don't you look for something better?
I'm trying to get me something to buy.
You know, between your job and what you make at Preservation Hall, you don't get to save
much money, do you? Not right now, I don't see. My money's probably going on, so my wife's been doing trips.
Oh, your wife's been making trips? Yeah. Where's she been going?
California.

Why don't you put a piano or a trumpet in her hand and make her earn some money like Sheik does when he goes home. Yeah. How many children do you have all together? Two boys. Two boys? How old are they?
My youngest boy is thirty, my oldest boy is thirty.
Hmm. Well, you have two dogs, huh?
Two dogs.

You've got one dog that runs away and just comes home at night to eat and the other one chews your shirts off the line. Chews my shirts off. You said the dog chewed another one of his shirts off and he'd better whip him again.
I didn't want to put the rose on this season. Then he didn't give him nothing either. That's the nice thing.
Oh, then he's going to eat your shirts some more and he's going to be hungry. You know, eat that wood out there.
You know, eat that.
What happened to all those cases of dog food you bought him? You built him a dog house? Yeah.
You know you've got a good house. You eat before I eat in the morning.
You stuff some way to keep them away.
The puppet has bit me already, man.
Well, on the days you're not working and the nights you're not playing at Preservation Hall, what do you do?
I go play bingo.
Where do you play bingo?
At St. Stephen's.
You ever won?
Yes, I won.
Yeah, what you win?
I won $40 one night. I won $40 one night. At Lady Conway on Luzin Avenue. I came back the next week for $130. I'm going to hit a bingo game.
Yeah, you do better on the bingo than you do on the horses, huh?
I don't play race.
You don't play race on the bingo? No, that's good. The only people who make money on the horses are the jockey. Do you have any hobbies or any other interests besides your music? That's what I like.
Music must seem at work. That's all I like.
That's all you like.
That's all.
Well, what other famous musicians have you played with besides the great Kid Cheek Koa? Well, Kid Thomas. And you made records. How many records have you made?
I made one recording with him.
Just that one with Kid Thomas? Is that the only recording you made?

That's all recording I made with that. Since I've been playing at the home. But I made records with Earl Fawcett, here's that. Then I made some recording on all these services. That recording, indeed. Then I made the recording with Cheek. Which one was that?
Oh, the Boston one, yeah. That was on that television show. When did you go in the service?
I went to the service in 1942.
In what branch?
Engineers.
Yeah? And what did you do there?
Huh?
What did you do in the engineering?
Play music.
You played the piano? Did they have a band?
I played for myself. I used to go play for the officers.
Oh, what? In the officers' club?
Played the officers' club.
You were proud?
I made more money playing in the home, and then I'm done doing all that.
Really? Are they paid you?

See, my canteen was my kidney cup. My canteen, where I used to drink out, was my kidney cup. Them guys started drinking that 7% beer down there. And I come home, my cup full of money, every night. Then I go to the PX and get that old 7% beer. But you had to be from the home to me to drink with you. I wouldn't afford the money to have.
What did you do? You just went in and played, like, just walked in and played and put your canteen up with the kids?
Put my canteen on the piano.
Oh, and then they'd come over and drop money?
Drop money in there.
What did they do, just sit around and listen to you?
Just sit around and listen to me.
Did you sing, too, while you were there? Yeah, I sang.
In fact, I was a movie projector. I made a movie. I showed the movies.
Oh, you did. How long did you stay in service?
Three years, too much. 22 days and five hours.
Yeah, exactly.
And I asked my company commander when there was the next bus leaving out for home.
Where were you stationed?
I stayed 16 months in the States.
Here in the States? Where?
I went to Mike Jimfield.
Where's that?
Down in Florida. All over Florida. Fort Myles, Sarasota, Tallahassee, Ole'Anna, St. Petersburg, Pensacola, Miami, then all over Florida. And then... Fort Chapel.
And then you went overseas?
Then I went from there to Dayton, Ohio. From there I went to Decent Mechanics School in the same hotel to Pure Illinois. I stayed there.
What did you learn there?

Decent Mechanics. I went to Decent Mechanics School at the Catterfield plant. From there they sent me back down to MacDill Field again. MacDill Field and sent me to Tallahassee, Florida. From there to Seattle, Washington at the Fort Emble location. Then we'll see.
Where'd you go? You went over to the Far East? To Japan?
Mm-hmm. Where'd you? Sicily, North Africa.
Oh, and you went out left from Seattle to go to Europe?
Yes, sir.
You went on a ship?
Ship. I went by plane.
Oh, you went by plane.
I caught a plane in Oklahoma.
Oh.
They rode me from Washington, D.C. to Oklahoma in one of them old cattle trucks. I caught a cattle truck.
Where were you stationed overseas first? I mean, where did you go first?
I went to Sicily.
And what did you do there?
Nothing. Nothing. There wasn't nothing to do now. I slept all day.
Oh, and what were you supposed to be doing?
I wasn't supposed to be working. I wasn't working.
Well, what were you supposed to be doing? What kind of work?
First place, they had me on, what do you call it? Peer them potatoes. I wasn't going to peel no potatoes.
That's K.P.?
K.P.
They sent you to diesel school so you could peel potatoes?
I didn't peel no potatoes.
What did you do?
I ate them potatoes.
With the skins on?
Sometimes I had baked potatoes, baked potatoes, you know, just baked them.
Potatoes treat under my day.
It was hard to know. They had to take your spoon in the way. It was hard to know.
And then where did you go after Sicily?
I went to Italy.
And what did you do there? Nothing again? What were you supposed to be doing?
I was supposed to have been working. When they looked for me, I went over here a couple times.
Well, I mean, what was your job in the Army, actually?
My job was supposed to have been a special service.
But for doing what?
Showing the movies.
Oh, that's all you were supposed to, that's all you did? Just show movies? Show movies,
that's all. I showed maybe one or two movies a week. And then my job was over.
And the rest of the time you just left?
That's right.
And how long did you stay overseas?
Twelve months.
And where else did you go besides Sicily and here and where else?
That's all.
That's all? And then you came back here?
Came back to the state. Came back to Hattiesburg and got this charge.
And then you came home?
Came home.
Well, when you learned something about diesels, did that help you with your mechanical law?

Neither one of them did help me because when I came back here, movement, had a gang of movement pitching machines operating at that time and I applied for a job and couldn't get a job nowhere. The man told me to put my name on the roster as a move projector operator. And I had to wiggle my name and somebody died for me to get a job as a move projector operator. Diesel mechanic, they wasn't allowing Negroes to operate at that time. Not diesel. But today you can do it. You can drive anything you want.
But that was to operate a diesel truck?
Yeah. I played all that. Ton of food, carry-offs, creepers, D4, D8, D12, I drove all that.
But you couldn't do it in civilian life?
Not in civilian life.
Did you do some of that in the Army?
I did, yeah, I worked like a dog. When you weren't loafing. I wasn't loafing. Did anybody else
play the music in your family?
My daddy played music. My daddy was a piccolo player. My daddy was the only piccolo player in the city. They called my daddy Mon-Gee.
Mon-Gee?
Mon-Gee was my daddy. My daddy played with Eddie Johnson. Eddie Johnson was my uncle. Played the bass.
He played a jazz piccolo? No, he played
a piccolo. Yeah, but he
played in jazz bands?
He played all the funnels in the parade.
Oh, really? I never heard of a piccolo player.
That's right.
What bands did he play with?
He played Eddie Johnson.
And who else?
Oh, Punch Miller. See Punch? Punch Miller was my auntie's first boyfriend.
Oh, really?
I used to go get a beer for Punch. and put drink some of the beer and put water in the bucket and bring it back in.
Is that why you stopped quoting your aunt?

When that time the show was a nickel. The show was a nickel. I used to shine the shoes. Sell the newspapers at the same time. I sold the newspapers to shine the shoes. I'd go out there on Sunday and say they'd make a dollar and a half, two dollars. My mama would give me fifteen cents out of my money. Out of my money. Didn't know what a new pair of shoes was. Every pair of shoes I wore was second hand.
Who got them first?
So my other had them before I got them. I'd go to the shoemaker and get me a pair. How much you want for them shoes? Twenty-five cents? Thirty cents? Get a good pair of shoes fifty cents. You know?
Oh, you bought you went and bought shoes from shoemaker. Shoemaker. No new shoes.
Never they went on new shoes until I got to be a man. That's right. Didn't know what overcoat was.
What'd you do in cold weather?

Staying inside. Staying inside. It was cold during that time. Then when I was a boy coming up my mama called herself to send me out in the country to live, Tibidale. Chicken eats a little egg. I used to be there and catch it when they get hot and soon he dropped it I had it. Oh. Boudin man passed by. Boudin, Boudin, Boudin, Boudin, Boudin. I said, yeah, he said, what you got? I said, I got two eggs. Take them two eggs and give me a big old hunk of Boudin.
What's Boudin?
That's blood size.
Oh. You swapped the eggs for that?
Swapped the eggs for that Boudin.

Me and that boudin at night, ate that boudin and... Drink some water. Huh? Drink me some water. No, go out there and steal me a quarter of milk. Where did you steal milk? Steal me a quarter of milk. And cream, bread, cream, bread, cream, bread, milk and boudin.
Where did you steal the milk?
Up the people's steps.
Oh.

I got out running a spidery with me. I knew I could run. Anytime I reached up and got my big apple off my head, I was gone. You couldn't catch me with a hound dog. Turn them callers doing 90 miles? No, turn them callers. Fell down with a bottle of milk in my hand one night. Pooleys got behind me one night. Fell down, broke the bottle. I stood there and had half of my hand. Went up there and started having the milk bottle. Quarter of milk.
I was just chasing you. I had a hard time. I was coming up.

See, I was raised with a step-four. My father died when I was five years old. My step-four used to cut my hair. Sometime he didn't cut it. Sometime my mama cut my hair. And sent me to school. I didn't go to school like real children did. Write on sleeve. Pencil. Chalked right with the chalk. And during that time people used to make shortcakes. I'd have shortcake. No bread, shortcake. Shortcake and Magnolia milk. Shortcake peanut butter. Shortcake blackberry jam. Going to school. And when you go to school, people do that at that time, you can ask for lining up. They give you a mammy cookie or a genius graham cracker, animal cake, something like that. I used to love to go to school.
Well you ate the shortcake for breakfast or you took it to school for lunch? I took that for my, that was my lunch. Better not eat it all. Better not eat it all.
Oh, you just ate part of it for breakfast and you saved the other? Yeah.
How many brothers and sisters did you have?

I got one brother can't whistle. Don't know how to whistle. Never, don't know no nothing but a river front. Why he works? He works out of the river front. Get out of the river front. Don't know no other ways but a river front. Been out there 26 years.
And how old is he?
He's year nine months old.
Is that your only brother or do you have?
Only brother.
Do you have any sisters?
I got step brothers and sisters.
How many of them?
I got a step brother. He's a game number one mechanic. But he won't fix my car.
Is he musically inclined in any way?

Well, he had a thing that go on one time. But I don't know, he got the devil in him, you know, try to buy a house. That got away from him. He tried to play piano but I told him, you know, I said I never seen a left hand piano play yet, man. I've never seen a left hand piano play, man. I've seen a right hand piano play, you know. I never seen a... Kim was on a left hand banjo play, I've seen.

Well, Sylvester Handy is based... He's left handed but he... The way he plays it, he puts his right hand around backwards somehow or other. You notice? He plays left handed because he's left handed but it's the way he holds the strings by twisting his hand around.
Kim was left handed too but he writes right handed.
He writes right handed, that's right. He writes right handed, that's right. Come to think of it, when he signed my book, I remember...
He writes right handed.
But he does everything else left handed.
Yeah, he writes right handed.

But, I know, I remember one night at Preservation Hall though, some guy came up, a white man, and he said to Kimble, You know, that's the first left handed banjo I've seen in a long time and I play banjo left handed.
